rounds.proof_sketch: num_features=64. Original: 1 block × 256 threads covers indices 0-63. Mutant: 1 block × 255 threads covers indices 0-63. Both sufficient. Moreover, update_running_stats_kernel executes AFTER output tensor is computed in apply_batchnorm_kernel, so running_stats changes cannot affect forward() return value.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation affects the block size for the update_running_stats_kernel from 256 to 255. With num_features=64, both configurations launch exactly 1 block that can process all 64 features correctly. More importantly, the running statistics update (Step 3) occurs AFTER the output tensor is computed (Step 2). The forward() method returns the output from Step 2, so any changes to running_mean/running_var buffers in Step 3 do not affect the returned tensor. The infection (different kernel launch parameters) does not propagate to the observable output.
rounds.kill_strategy: UNKILLABLE under single-call fixed-shape testing. The mutation only affects internal buffer updates that occur after output computation. To kill this mutant would require: (1) multi-call testing where running_stats from training affect subsequent eval-mode outputs, or (2) explicit inspection of running_mean/running_var buffers, or (3) num_features > 255 so block count differs.
rounds.recommendations: When testing batch normalization kernels, consider testing both the output tensor AND the updated running statistics separately. Also test multi-call scenarios where training-mode updates affect subsequent inference-mode outputs. The mutation testing framework should track buffer side-effects, not just return values.
